bib.title: Clean Code, Chapter 1: Clean Code
bib.venue: Prentice Hall (book: Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship)

question: Why does code quality matter, who is responsible for it, and what does it mean for code to be clean?

results.claim: Martin asserts that the ratio of time spent reading code to writing it is well over 10:1, based on his recollection of replaying editor sessions, with no study cited.
results.setup: Anecdote from replaying Emacs keystroke sessions in the 80s and 90s; no sample size, no method, no citation.
results.quote: Indeed, the ratio of time spent reading vs. writing is well over 10:1.

results.claim: A company that shipped a popular late-80s app went out of business because rushed, messy code made release cycles stretch and bugs go unfixed.
results.setup: Single unnamed company, told second-hand by a former employee two decades later.
results.quote: It was the bad code that brought the company down.

results.claim: Ron Jeffries gives Beck's four rules of simple code, in priority order: runs all tests, no duplication, expresses all design ideas, minimises entities.
results.source: Ron Jeffries, quoting Kent Beck's rules of simple code
results.setup: Opinion quoted from Jeffries; four rules in priority order.
results.note: The list items are on the following lines (p. 10).

limits: Opinion and anecdote throughout; no measurement. The 10:1 reading ratio and the company-failure story are unsupported by data.
The author says the recommendations are one school of thought, not absolute truth, and that 'many of the recommendations in this book are controversial' (p. 13).
Chapter is introductory: it defines no concrete rules for naming, function size or comments (those come in later chapters). The productivity-vs-time curve (Fig 1-1) is illustrative, not data.
Ousterhout disputes some later Clean Code positions (function size, comments); this chapter does not take them up.
practices: Keep code clean at all times, because messes slow you down immediately and cleaning later never happens ('Later equals never'; p. 4, p. 6).
Make code easy to read even at some cost to writing, because reading dominates and surrounding code must be read to write new code (p. 14).

Apply the Boy Scout Rule: leave the code a little cleaner than you found it with small changes such as renaming a variable, splitting a function, removing duplication or simplifying a conditional (p. 14).
Defend the code against schedule pressure the way a doctor refuses to skip hand-washing; programmers share responsibility for bad code (p. 5-6).
Remove duplication, express design ideas with meaningful names, and apply Extract Method so a method says what it does and submethods say how (Jeffries, p. 10-11).
Wrap implementation details such as 'find things in a collection' in a small abstraction so the implementation can change later (Jeffries, p. 11).
Clean code has unit and acceptance tests; code without tests is not clean (Big Dave Thomas, p. 9).
Handle errors completely and attend to detail; inconsistent naming and abbreviated error handling are signs of inattention (Stroustrup, p. 8).

terms.definition: Being significantly impeded by bad code: 'We wade through bad code.'
A painstakingly acquired sense of cleanliness that lets a programmer see options and plan a sequence of behavior-preserving transformations from messy to clean code.
Thomas and Hunt: visible neglect in one place makes others stop caring, so decay spreads.
Leave the campground cleaner than you found it.
A tiger-team rewrite that must match the old system while it keeps changing; Martin says he has seen it take 10 years.

Stroustrup: elegant, efficient, does one thing well. Booch: simple and direct, reads like prose. Thomas: readable and changeable by others, tested, minimal. Feathers: written by someone who cares. Jeffries: no duplication, expressive, tiny abstractions. Cunningham: each routine is pretty much what you expected.

lineage.note: Martin disputes its preface calling good code a 'fragile premise'.
